roomSize.description: Simulated room size. Range: 0.0–1.0. Scales the comb filter delay lengths and feedback coefficient (0.7 at roomSize=0, 0.98 at roomSize=1). Larger values produce longer, more diffuse reverberation tails.

damping.description: High-frequency damping in the comb filter feedback loops. Range: 0.0–1.0. Higher values attenuate high frequencies faster, simulating sound-absorbing room surfaces.

mix.description: Dry/wet mix ratio. Range: 0.0–1.0. 0 = fully dry (no reverb), 0.3 = subtle room ambience, 1.0 = fully wet (100% reverb).

examples.title: Room ambience
examples.description: AudioFile → Reverb(roomSize=0.5, damping=0.4, mix=0.25) → Speaker Adds natural room reverberation to a dry recording.

examples.title: Large hall effect
examples.description: Sine(440 Hz) → Reverb(roomSize=0.9, damping=0.2, mix=0.7) → Oscilloscope Long decay tail visible on the oscilloscope after the sine is muted.

quantizer.title: Quantizer (ADC Emulator)
quantizer.purpose: Quantises the input signal to a finite number of levels corresponding to an N-bit ADC. Allows studying quantisation noise, staircase distortion, and the effect of bit-depth reduction on signal quality — important for fixed-point DSP design and audio dithering.
quantizer.algorithm: The number of quantisation levels is L = 2^bits. The input is clamped to [−1, 1]. Two modes: Mid-rise (no zero level): the positive and negative halves each contain L/2 levels, output = (floor(x · L/2) + 0.5) / (L/2). Mid-tread (zero level present): output = round(x · (L/2 − 1)) / (L/2 − 1), which places a quantisation level exactly at zero. The output is clamped to [−1, 1].
quantizer.inputDescription: real (Float32Array of length chunkSize, values should be in [−1, 1] for meaningful results)
quantizer.outputDescription: real (Float32Array — quantised signal with values on a uniform grid of 2^bits levels)

bits.description: Number of quantisation bits. Range: 1–16. 1 bit = 2 levels (comparator), 8 bits = 256 levels (CD-quality at low rate), 16 bits = 65536 levels (CD audio). Each additional bit adds 6 dB of dynamic range.

quantizerType.description: 'mid-tread' — quantisation levels include zero (standard for most ADC designs). 'mid-rise' — levels are offset by half a step so zero is not representable (common in two's-complement ADCs).

examples.title: Quantisation noise spectrum
examples.description: Sine(997 Hz) → Quantizer(bits=4, mid-tread) → SpectrumAnalyzer With 4-bit quantisation, harmonic distortion products are visible at harmonics of 997 Hz.

examples.title: Bit-depth comparison
examples.description: AudioFile → Quantizer(bits=3) → Speaker Degraded 3-bit audio demonstrates the audible granular noise of low-resolution quantisation.

sample-hold.title: Sample and Hold
sample-hold.purpose: Emulates a sample-and-hold (S&H) circuit that samples the input at regular intervals and holds the value until the next sample. Used to demonstrate aliasing and the effect of reduced effective sample rate; also models zero-order hold (ZOH) reconstruction in DAC analysis.
sample-hold.algorithm: An internal counter increments each sample. When it reaches zero (at the start of each period), the current input value is latched into heldValue. The output equals heldValue for all samples in the period. The counter wraps from holdPeriod − 1 to 0.
sample-hold.outputDescription: real (Float32Array — staircase waveform: constant within each holdPeriod-sample interval)

holdPeriod.description: Sampling period in samples. 1 = pass-through (no effect). 10 = sample every 10th input value, creating a staircase with steps 10 samples wide. At 48000 Hz, holdPeriod=480 samples the signal at 100 Hz.

examples.title: Aliasing demonstration
examples.description: Sine(1000 Hz) → SampleHold(holdPeriod=24) → SpectrumAnalyzer The effective sample rate is 48000/24 = 2000 Hz; the 1000 Hz signal is at the Nyquist limit, producing a very degraded output.

examples.title: Staircase waveform
examples.description: Sine(100 Hz) → SampleHold(holdPeriod=48) → Oscilloscope A coarsely sampled staircase approximation of the sine wave is visible.

convolution.title: Convolution
convolution.purpose: Computes the linear convolution of two signals: y[n] = Σ x₁[k] · x₂[n−k]. Convolution is the fundamental operation linking a system's input to its output via the impulse response. This block is used for manual FIR filtering, cross-correlation experiments, and demonstrating the convolution theorem.
convolution.algorithm: Direct (brute-force) convolution in 'same' mode: the output length equals the input signal length. The kernel is aligned at its centre (halfKer = floor(kerLen / 2)) so the zero-delay sample is centred. For each output index n, the sum runs over all kernel taps k where the input index (n − halfKer + k) is valid. Optional energy normalisation divides each output sample by √(Σ kernel²) to make the result independent of kernel scale.
convolution.inputDescription: - Input 0: real — signal x₁ (the primary input). - Input 1: real — kernel x₂ (typically the impulse response or matched filter template).
convolution.outputDescription: real (Float32Array of length chunkSize — convolution result in 'same' mode)

normalize.description: When true, the output is divided by the square root of the kernel energy, making the result independent of the kernel's absolute scale. Useful when comparing convolutions with different kernel magnitudes.

examples.title: Manual FIR filtering
examples.description: Sine(2000 Hz) → Convolution ← Impulse → LowpassFIR → [as kernel input]; Convolution output → Oscilloscope. Demonstrates that convolving a signal with the FIR impulse response is equivalent to filtering.

examples.title: Cross-correlation
examples.description: Signal → Convolution(input 0) ← time-reversed template (input 1) Convolution with a time-reversed template computes cross-correlation, equivalent to matched filtering.

wavelet-transform.title: Wavelet Transform (Haar DWT)
wavelet-transform.purpose: Computes the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) using the Haar wavelet, decomposing the signal into approximation and detail coefficients at multiple scales. Unlike the FFT which has fixed time-frequency resolution, the DWT provides good time resolution at high frequencies and good frequency resolution at low frequencies — ideal for analysing transients, detecting discontinuities, and multi-scale signal analysis.
wavelet-transform.algorithm: 1. The input is zero-padded to the next power of 2. 2. At each of the 'levels' decomposition levels, the current array is split into: cA[k] = (x[2k] + x[2k+1]) / √2 (low-pass) and cD[k] = (x[2k] − x[2k+1]) / √2 (high-pass). 3. The detail coefficients cD are saved; the approximation cA is fed to the next level. 4. The output is packed as [cA_L | cD_L | cD_{L−1} | … | cD_1], where cA_L is the coarsest approximation and cD_1 are the finest-scale details.
wavelet-transform.outputDescription: real (Float32Array of length chunkSize — DWT coefficients in standard packing: [cA_L | cD_L | … | cD_1])

levels.description: Number of decomposition levels. Range: 1 to log₂(chunkSize). Level 1 produces 2 sub-bands; level 3 produces 4. More levels reveal lower-frequency detail but reduce time resolution for the approximation.

wavelet.description: Wavelet basis. Currently only 'haar' is supported. The Haar wavelet is the simplest orthogonal wavelet and is equivalent to a two-tap averaging and differencing filter bank.

examples.title: Multi-scale analysis
examples.description: Sine(100 Hz) → WaveletTransform(levels=3) → Oscilloscope The packed coefficients show energy concentrated in the cA_3 (approximation) region.

examples.title: Transient detection
examples.description: Step(stepTime=0.01 s) → WaveletTransform(levels=4) → Oscilloscope A spike in the detail coefficients (cD bands) marks the position of the step.

cepstrum.title: Cepstrum
cepstrum.purpose: Computes the real cepstrum of the input signal: c[n] = Re(IFFT(log(|FFT(x)|²))). The cepstrum operates in the 'quefrency' domain, where periodicities in the spectrum (caused by harmonics, echoes, or source-filter separation) appear as peaks. Applications include pitch detection, echo detection, and speech source-filter analysis.
cepstrum.algorithm: 1. A Hann window is applied to the input chunk to reduce spectral leakage. 2. The windowed signal is zero-padded to the next power of 2. 3. FFT is computed. 4. Log power spectrum: log(|X[k]|² + ε) is computed for each bin (ε = 1e-20 prevents log(0)). 5. IFFT of the log spectrum is computed. 6. The real part of the result is the real cepstrum. Peaks in the output at quefrency q correspond to periodicities with period q samples in the frequency domain, i.e., a fundamental frequency of sampleRate / q Hz.
cepstrum.outputDescription: real (Float32Array of length chunkSize — cepstral coefficients in quefrency order; quefrency index q corresponds to frequency sampleRate/q Hz)

windowSize.description: Analysis window length in samples. The FFT is performed on min(windowSize, chunkSize) samples zero-padded to the next power of 2. Larger windows give finer quefrency resolution. Default: 1024.

examples.title: Pitch detection via cepstrum
examples.description: Sine(440 Hz) → Cepstrum(windowSize=2048) → Oscilloscope A peak appears at quefrency ≈ 48000/440 ≈ 109 samples, corresponding to the 440 Hz pitch.

examples.title: Echo delay measurement
examples.description: Sine(1000 Hz) + DelayLine(200 samples, gain=0.5) → Cepstrum → Oscilloscope A peak at quefrency 200 reveals the echo delay.

power-meter.title: Power Meter
power-meter.purpose: Measures the power of the input signal and displays RMS level, peak level, average absolute value, and dBFS (decibels relative to full scale). This is a standard measurement block for audio level metering and signal power monitoring.
power-meter.algorithm: For each chunk: RMS = √(Σ x²[n] / N); peak = max(|x[n]|); average = Σ |x[n]| / N; dBFS = 20·log₁₀(RMS). The measurements are returned as a data object for display in the visualisation panel. No state is retained between chunks — each chunk is measured independently.
power-meter.outputDescription: none (visualisation block — displays RMS, peak, average, and dBFS in the block panel)

examples.title: Signal level monitoring
examples.description: Sine(1000 Hz, amplitude=0.5) → PowerMeter Expected RMS ≈ 0.354 (0.5/√2), dBFS ≈ −9 dB.

examples.title: Noise power measurement
examples.description: NoiseGenerator(white, amplitude=0.1) → PowerMeter Measures the actual RMS of the white noise generator output.

snr-meter.title: SNR Meter
snr-meter.purpose: Measures the Signal-to-Noise Ratio in dB by comparing a noisy signal with a clean reference signal. The noise is estimated as the difference between the two inputs: noise = signal − reference. This block is useful for evaluating the performance of noise reduction, channel coding, or any block that modifies signal quality.
snr-meter.algorithm: For each chunk, the reference power P_ref = Σ ref²[n] / N and the noise power P_noise = Σ (sig[n] − ref[n])² / N are computed. SNR = 10·log₁₀(P_ref / P_noise) dB. If P_noise < 1e-20, SNR is reported as Infinity. Both inputs must be connected for a valid measurement.
snr-meter.inputDescription: - Input 0 'Signal': real — the noisy or processed signal. - Input 1 'Reference': real — the clean reference signal (ideally the same signal before degradation).
snr-meter.outputDescription: none (visualisation block — displays SNR in dB, signal power, and noise power)

examples.title: Measuring channel SNR
examples.description: Sine(1000 Hz) → [SNR Input 0 (noisy)]; Sine(1000 Hz) → AWGNChannel(SNR=15 dB) → [SNR Input 0]; Sine(1000 Hz) → [SNR Reference Input 1]; SNRMeter displays the actual SNR of the AWGN channel.

examples.title: Filter SNR improvement
examples.description: Sine(500 Hz) → AWGNChannel(SNR=5 dB) → LowpassFIR(cutoff 1000 Hz) → [SNRMeter signal]; Sine(500 Hz) → [SNRMeter reference]; The filter narrows the noise bandwidth and the measured SNR increases.

ber-counter.title: BER Counter
ber-counter.purpose: Measures the Bit Error Rate (BER) by comparing transmitted and received bit streams sample by sample. BER is the primary performance metric for digital communication systems. The block accumulates bit decisions over the entire simulation run to provide a statistically reliable estimate.
ber-counter.algorithm: Each input sample is thresholded to a binary decision: bit = 1 if value > threshold, else 0. The Tx (input 0) and Rx (input 1) bits are compared; any mismatch is counted as an error. Cumulative counters state.totalBits and state.errorBits are maintained across chunks. BER = errorBits / totalBits. The state is cleared when the simulation is reset.
ber-counter.inputDescription: - Input 0 'Tx': real — transmitted bit stream (from modulator or reference). - Input 1 'Rx': real — received bit stream (from demodulator after the channel).
ber-counter.outputDescription: none (visualisation block — displays BER, total bits counted, and error bit count)

threshold.description: Decision threshold for binarising each sample. Samples above threshold are treated as a '1' bit, samples below as '0'. Default: 0.5 (suitable for signals normalised to [0, 1]).

examples.title: 16-QAM BER measurement
examples.description: QAMModulator(16QAM) → AWGNChannel(SNR=15 dB) → QAMDemodulator(hard) → [BER Rx]; QAMModulator (clean copy) → [BER Tx]; BERCounter displays the measured BER.

examples.title: BER vs SNR sweep
examples.description: Change the AWGN SNR from 5 to 30 dB in steps, restarting the simulation each time, and record the BER from BERCounter to build a BER curve.

histogram.title: Histogram
histogram.purpose: Displays the amplitude distribution (probability density function estimate) of the input signal. The histogram shape reveals the statistical nature of the signal: Gaussian noise produces a bell curve, uniform noise produces a flat rectangle, a pure sine produces a U-shaped arcsine distribution.
histogram.algorithm: For each chunk the minimum and maximum values are found. The amplitude range is divided into numBins equal-width bins. Each sample is assigned to a bin: idx = floor((x − min) / binWidth). The bin counts are normalised by the chunk size to give a fraction-of-total representation. The range is expanded by ±0.5 if all samples are identical to prevent division by zero.
histogram.outputDescription: none (visualisation block — displays a bar chart of amplitude distribution)

bins.description: Number of histogram bins. Range: 4–256. More bins give finer amplitude resolution but require more data for smooth estimates. Default: 64.

examples.title: Gaussian noise distribution
examples.description: NoiseGenerator(white, Gaussian via AWGN trick) → Histogram(bins=64) The histogram shows a bell curve, confirming Gaussian amplitude distribution.

examples.title: Comparing signal distributions
examples.description: Sine(1000 Hz) → Histogram(bins=64) Sine wave produces the characteristic arcsine (U-shaped) distribution with peaks near ±amplitude.

eye-diagram.title: Eye Diagram
eye-diagram.purpose: Displays the eye diagram of a digital signal by overlaying consecutive symbol intervals on a single plot. An open 'eye' indicates low inter-symbol interference (ISI) and good timing margin; a closed or distorted eye indicates ISI, noise, or timing jitter. The eye diagram is the standard tool for evaluating digital communication link quality.
eye-diagram.algorithm: The input chunk is divided into non-overlapping segments of samplesPerSymbol length. Two symbol periods (2 × samplesPerSymbol samples) are captured per trace to show the full symbol transition pattern. Each trace is stored as a separate Float32Array and passed to the visualisation component, which overlays them on a single time axis. The number of displayed traces is floor(chunkSize / samplesPerSymbol).
eye-diagram.inputDescription: real (Float32Array of length chunkSize — baseband signal after the receive filter, before the decision device)
eye-diagram.outputDescription: none (visualisation block — displays overlaid symbol traces)

samplesPerSymbol.description: Number of samples per modulation symbol. Must match the transmitter's oversampling rate. For a symbol rate of 1000 baud at 48000 Hz sample rate, set samplesPerSymbol = 48. Range: 2 and above.

examples.title: Eye diagram after pulse shaping
examples.description: QAMModulator(symbolRate=1000) → PulseShaper(RRC, sps=4) → [real part via RealPart] → EyeDiagram(samplesPerSymbol=4) A wide-open eye confirms ISI-free transmission at the optimal sampling instant.

examples.title: ISI effect visualisation
examples.description: QAMModulator(symbolRate=1000) → MultipathChannel(delays='0,2', gains='1.0,0.5') → EyeDiagram(sps=48) The eye closes due to inter-symbol interference from the multipath channel.

thd-meter.title: THD Meter
thd-meter.purpose: Measures Total Harmonic Distortion (THD) of the input signal — the ratio of the power in all harmonic components to the power of the fundamental frequency. THD is the key metric for evaluating the linearity of amplifiers, ADCs, DACs, and nonlinear DSP systems.
thd-meter.algorithm: 1. The input is zero-padded or truncated to fftSize and an FFT is performed. 2. The magnitudes of all positive-frequency bins are computed. 3. The fundamental is the bin with maximum magnitude (DC excluded). 4. For each harmonic h = 2, 3, 4, … up to the Nyquist bin, the magnitude at bin h·fundBin is collected. 5. THD = √(Σ harmonic_magnitudes²) / fundamental_magnitude × 100%. 6. THD in dB = 20·log₁₀(THD/100). Output includes fundamental frequency, THD%, THD dB, and an array of harmonic frequencies and magnitudes.
thd-meter.inputDescription: real (Float32Array of length chunkSize — signal whose harmonic content is to be measured)
thd-meter.outputDescription: none (visualisation block — displays fundamental frequency, THD%, THD dB, and harmonic table)

fftSize.description: FFT size for harmonic analysis. Larger values improve frequency resolution (Δf = sampleRate/fftSize) and reduce harmonic overlap. Must be a power of 2. Default: 4096 gives Δf ≈ 11.7 Hz at 48000 Hz.

examples.title: Amplifier distortion test
examples.description: Sine(1000 Hz) → [nonlinear block / Compressor] → THDMeter(fftSize=4096) Measures how much harmonic distortion the nonlinear processing introduces.

examples.title: Clean signal baseline
examples.description: Sine(1000 Hz, amplitude=0.5) → THDMeter The ideal sine should show THD below 0.01% (limited by floating-point precision).

pole-zero-diagram.title: Pole-Zero Diagram
pole-zero-diagram.purpose: A parametric visualisation block that computes and displays the poles and zeros of a discrete-time transfer function H(z) = B(z)/A(z) from user-supplied polynomial coefficients. The pole-zero plot is the primary tool for analysing filter stability, frequency response shape, and phase characteristics.
pole-zero-diagram.algorithm: The numerator (zeros) and denominator (poles) coefficient strings are parsed into numeric arrays. Roots are found analytically for polynomials of degree ≤ 2 (linear equation, quadratic formula). For degree ≥ 3 the Durand-Kerner iterative method initialises N guesses on the unit circle and converges to the roots of the monic polynomial. Stability is determined by checking that all poles satisfy |p| < 1.0 (inside the unit circle).
pole-zero-diagram.outputDescription: none (visualisation block — displays poles (×) and zeros (○) on the complex z-plane with the unit circle)

numerator.description: Coefficients of the numerator polynomial B(z), comma-separated in descending power order: 'b0, b1, b2, …'. Example: '1,0,-1' represents B(z) = 1 − z⁻². The roots of B(z) are the zeros of H(z).

denominator.description: Coefficients of the denominator polynomial A(z), comma-separated. Example: '1,-1.5,0.7' represents A(z) = 1 − 1.5z⁻¹ + 0.7z⁻². The roots of A(z) are the poles of H(z).

examples.title: Second-order IIR filter analysis
examples.description: PoleZeroDiagram(numerator='1,0,-1', denominator='1,-1.5,0.7') Shows two zeros on the real axis and a complex pole pair inside the unit circle (stable filter).

examples.title: Stability boundary check
examples.description: Set denominator='1,-1.8,0.95' to place poles near the unit circle. The diagram shows the poles almost touching the unit circle, indicating a highly resonant (but stable) filter.

phase-portrait.title: Phase Portrait
phase-portrait.purpose: Visualises the trajectory of a complex signal in the I-Q (state space) plane. Unlike the Constellation diagram which shows discrete symbol samples, the phase portrait shows the continuous signal path, revealing the dynamics of a modulated signal, the attractor of a nonlinear system, or the trajectory of a PLL during acquisition.
phase-portrait.algorithm: The block is a transparent passthrough: it receives the complex I/Q input, passes the raw interleaved Float32Array directly to the visualisation component, and returns it without modification. The visualisation component plots I (horizontal) vs Q (vertical) for the last trailLength samples, fading older points.
phase-portrait.inputDescription: complex (interleaved Float32Array of length chunkSize × 2 — I/Q signal to be plotted)
phase-portrait.outputDescription: none (visualisation block — displays I vs Q scatter/trajectory plot)

trailLength.description: Number of most recent I/Q samples to display. Longer trails show more history but can obscure recent trajectory. Default: 2048.

dotSize.description: Radius of each plotted point in pixels. Larger dots are easier to see for sparse constellations; smaller dots give finer trajectory detail. Default: 2.

examples.title: QPSK signal trajectory
examples.description: PSKModulator(QPSK, fc=1000 Hz) → PhasePortrait The trajectory shows the four constellation points connected by the inter-symbol transition paths.

examples.title: PLL acquisition trajectory
examples.description: Sine(1050 Hz) → ComplexComposer → CarrierRecovery(fc=1000, BW=100) → [NCO output] → PhasePortrait The NCO trajectory spirals inward to the unit circle as the loop acquires lock.

group-delay-plot.title: Group Delay Plot
group-delay-plot.purpose: Computes and displays the group delay of the input signal as a function of frequency. Group delay τ(f) = −dφ/dω is the frequency-dependent propagation delay of a signal's envelope through a system. Non-constant group delay (group delay distortion) causes different frequency components to arrive at different times, which is audible as phase distortion and degrades digital communication eye diagrams.
group-delay-plot.algorithm: 1. The input chunk is zero-padded/truncated to fftSize and FFT-transformed. 2. The phase φ[k] = atan2(imag[k], real[k]) is computed for each positive-frequency bin. 3. Phase unwrapping corrects 2π jumps between consecutive bins. 4. Group delay is estimated by finite difference: τ[k] = −(φ[k] − φ[k−1]) / (2π/N), where 2π/N is the angular frequency step between bins. Results are returned in samples; multiply by 1/sampleRate to convert to seconds.
group-delay-plot.inputDescription: real (Float32Array of length chunkSize — typically the output of a filter whose group delay is to be measured, driven by a broadband signal such as white noise or a chirp)
group-delay-plot.outputDescription: none (visualisation block — displays group delay in samples vs frequency in Hz)

fftSize.description: FFT size for analysis. Larger values give finer frequency resolution (Δf = sampleRate/fftSize) but average over a longer time window. Default: 1024.

examples.title: Linear-phase FIR group delay
examples.description: NoiseGenerator(white) → LowpassFIR(cutoff 2000 Hz, 64 taps) → GroupDelayPlot(fftSize=1024) A linear-phase FIR filter shows constant group delay (flat horizontal line) in the passband.

examples.title: IIR phase distortion
examples.description: NoiseGenerator(white) → IIRFilter(Butterworth lowpass) → GroupDelayPlot The Butterworth filter shows large group delay variation near the cutoff frequency.

allpass-filter.title: Allpass Filter
allpass-filter.purpose: A filter with unity magnitude response (|H(f)| = 1 for all frequencies) that modifies only the phase relationships between frequency components. Allpass filters are building blocks of phase equalisers, reverberation algorithms, phaser effects, and group delay correction. Unlike conventional filters, they do not attenuate or boost any frequency — they only shift phase.
allpass-filter.algorithm: A cascade of 2nd-order biquad sections is used. Each section implements an allpass design: w₀ = 2π·fc/fs; α = sin(w₀)/(2Q); b₀ = (1−α)/a₀; b₁ = −2cos(w₀)/a₀; b₂ = (1+α)/a₀ = a₂_normalised; a₁ = −2cos(w₀)/a₀; a₂ = (1−α)/a₀ (note: for allpass b0 = a2_norm and b2 = a0_norm). The number of sections is floor(order/2). Cascading sections increases the total phase swing by 360° per section near the centre frequency.
allpass-filter.outputDescription: real (Float32Array — phase-shifted signal with identical amplitude to the input)

centerFrequency.description: Centre frequency of the phase transition in Hz. At this frequency a single 2nd-order section produces a phase shift of −180°. Range: 1 Hz to sampleRate/2.

bandwidth.description: Q factor controlling the sharpness of the phase transition. Higher Q gives a steeper phase transition concentrated near the centre frequency. Low Q (< 0.5) gives a very gradual phase shift spread across a wide frequency range.

order.description: Filter order — must be even. Number of biquad sections = order/2. Each section adds 360° of total phase swing near the centre frequency. Range: 2–20. Default: 2 (one biquad section, −360° total phase range).

examples.title: Phaser audio effect
examples.description: AudioFile → AllpassFilter(fc=500 Hz, Q=1.0, order=4) → Summer(with dry signal) → Speaker Mixing the allpass output with the dry signal creates notches in the spectrum characteristic of a phaser effect.

examples.title: Group delay correction
examples.description: Signal → IIRFilter(lowpass) → AllpassFilter(fc=1000 Hz, Q=0.7, order=2) → GroupDelayPlot The allpass compensates for the non-linear phase of the IIR filter, flattening the group delay.
